hello.title: Hello, Haskell!
hello.summary: Write your first Haskell program, print text and numbers, and run several actions in a do block.
hello.lesson.0: Every Haskell program starts at `main`. `putStrLn` prints a text and then a line break. In Haskell, a text is called a `String` and goes in double quotes.
hello.lesson.2: The first line is a **type signature**. `main :: IO ()` says that `main` is an action that does input or output. You could leave this line out, but it is good style to write it.
hello.lesson.4: To run several actions one after the other, write `do` and put the actions below it, each on its own line. All lines of a `do` block must start in the same column, so indent them by the same number of spaces.
hello.lesson.7: `putStr` prints a text without a line break. `print` prints any value, for example a number. When you `print` a text, it shows the quotes.
hello.lesson.9: `++` joins two strings. `show` turns a number into a string, so you can join it with a text. Parentheses group what belongs together: `putStrLn ("Age: " ++ show 36)` prints the joined text.
hello.lesson.11: Without the parentheses, `putStrLn "Age: " ++ show 36` is an error. Haskell reads it as `(putStrLn "Age: ") ++ show 36` and reports a type error.
hello.lesson.12: Haskell ignores everything from `--` to the end of the line. This is a **comment**, a note for people who read the code.
hello.card.0: `main :: IO ()` is where the program starts
hello-1.prompt: Where does a Haskell program start?
hello-1.options.0: At the first line of the file
hello-1.options.3: At the last line of the file
hello-1.explain: The program runs the action `main`. It can be anywhere in the file.
hello-2.explain: `putStr` adds no line break, so `morning` follows on the same line.
hello-4.explain: `print` shows a text the way you write it in code, with double quotes. `putStrLn` would print it without quotes.
hello-5.statement: `putStr` prints a line break after the text.
hello-5.explain: `putStr` prints the text only. `putStrLn` adds the line break.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Score: 10.
hello-6.explain: `++` joins two strings. `+` only adds numbers.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints A and B on two lines.
hello-7.explain: `do` starts a block of actions that run one after the other.
hello-8.prompt: Build a program that prints Hello.
hello-8.explain: `main = putStrLn "Hello"` defines `main` as the action that prints `Hello`. `==` compares values.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Start, 3 and End on three lines.
hello-9.explain: `main = do` comes first. The actions below it run from top to bottom.
hello-10.prompt: The program should print Name: Ada and Age: 36. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: `++` joins strings, and `36` is a number. Convert it first: `putStrLn ("Age: " ++ show 36)`.
hello-11.prompt: The program should print One, Two and Three. Which line has the bug?
hello-11.explain: All lines of a `do` block must start in the same column. Indent the line by four spaces like the others.
hello-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-12.pairs.0: prints a text and a line break
hello-12.pairs.1: prints a text without a line break
hello-12.pairs.3: turns a value into a string
values.title: Values and types
values.summary: Give values a name and get to know the types Int, Double, Bool, Char and String.
values.lesson.0: In Haskell, you give a value a **name** with `=`. A name always keeps its value: you cannot change it later. So `=` is a definition, not an assignment. Names start with a lowercase letter.
values.lesson.3: Every value has a **type**. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` is a number with a decimal point, and `Bool` is `True` or `False`. `Char` is a single character in single quotes, and `String` is a text in double quotes. Types start with an uppercase letter.
values.lesson.6: `+`, `-` and `*` work as usual, and `^` raises to a power. `/` divides and gives a number with decimals. For whole numbers, write `div` before the two numbers to get the whole part of the division, and `mod` to get the remainder.
values.lesson.8: Inside a `do` block, `let` gives a name to a value. You can use the name in the lines below.
values.lesson.11: Haskell never mixes types on its own. To use an `Int` in a calculation with a `Double`, convert it with `fromIntegral`. To join a number with a text, convert it with `show`.
values.lesson.13: If `count` is an `Int`, `count / 2` is an error, because `/` needs a type with decimals, such as `Double`. Write `div count 2` or `fromIntegral count / 2` instead.
values.card.0: `x = 5` defines a name that never changes
values-1.explain: `div` gives the whole part of the division: 17 / 5 is 3 with a remainder of 2.
values-3.explain: `/` divides with decimals. For the whole part, you would use `div`.
values-4.prompt: Which type does the value `'x'` have?
values-4.explain: Single quotes mark a single character, a `Char`. A `String` uses double quotes.
values-5.statement: After `count = 3`, you can write `count = 4` later in the same program to change the value.
values-5.explain: A name in Haskell keeps its value. Defining `count` twice is an error.
values-6.statement: `True` and `False` are the two values of the type `Bool`.
values-6.explain: A `Bool` is either `True` or `False`. Both start with an uppercase letter.
values-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 2.5.
values-7.explain: `fromIntegral` converts the `Int` so that `/` can use it. `show` would make a `String`.
values-8.explain: A text in double quotes is a `String`. Types start with an uppercase letter.
values-9.prompt: Inside a do block, build the line that names the result of 3 times 4 total.
values-9.explain: `let total = 3 * 4` gives the result the name `total` for the following lines.
values-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 20.
values-10.explain: `b` uses `a`, so `a` must be defined first. `print b` comes last.
values-11.prompt: The program should print 3, the whole part of 7 divided by 2. Which line has the bug?
values-11.explain: `/` does not work with an `Int`. Use `div` for whole numbers: `main = print (div count 2)`.
values-12.prompt: Match the type with its values.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Define your own functions with parameters and type signatures, and call them with arguments.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** takes values and gives back a result. You define it with its name, the names of its parameters, `=` and the result. To call it, write the function name and then the arguments, separated by spaces, without parentheses or commas.
functions.lesson.2: The type signature `Int -> Int` means: the function takes an `Int` and gives back an `Int`. With two parameters, the signature has two arrows. The last type is always the type of the result.
functions.lesson.5: A function call binds more strongly than any operator: `double 3 + 1` means `(double 3) + 1`. If an argument is a calculation or another call, put it in parentheses, as in `double (3 + 1)`.
functions.lesson.7: Functions work with all types. This function takes a `String` and gives back a new `String`.
functions.lesson.10: `where` after a function defines helper names that only this function can use. Inside a `do` block, `let` can also define a small function, for example `let triple x = x * 3`.
functions.lesson.12: Do not put commas between arguments. `area 3 4` is right. `area (3, 4)` passes a single value made of two numbers and gives a type error.
functions.lesson.13: A function like `double` computes its result only from its arguments. With the same arguments, it always gives back the same result.
functions-2.explain: The call binds more strongly than `*`: `add 2 3` is `5`, and `5 * 10` is `50`.
functions-3.explain: `square 2 + 1` means `(square 2) + 1`, so 4 + 1 = 5. For `9`, you would write `square (2 + 1)`.
functions-4.prompt: What does the type `Int -> Int -> Bool` describe?
functions-4.options.0: A function that takes two `Int` values and gives back a `Bool`
functions-4.options.1: A function that takes a `Bool` and gives back two `Int` values
functions-4.options.2: A list of two `Int` values and a `Bool`
functions-4.options.3: A function that takes three values
functions-4.explain: The last type after the arrows is the result. The types before it are the parameters.
functions-6.prompt: Complete the function so that half 10 gives 5.
functions-6.explain: `div n 2` divides two whole numbers. `mod` would give the remainder, `0`.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hi, Ada.
functions-7.explain: Without parentheses, `putStrLn` would get two arguments, `greet` and `"Ada"`. The parentheses pass it the result of the call.
functions-8.prompt: Build a function inc that adds 1 to its argument.
functions-8.explain: First the name and the parameter, then `=` and the result `x + 1`. Haskell has no `return` for this.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 10.
functions-9.explain: `result` uses the function `double`, so `double` must be defined first.
functions-10.prompt: The program should print 5. Which line has the bug?
functions-10.explain: Arguments are separated by spaces, not by commas: `main = print (add 2 3)`.
functions-11.prompt: The program should print Hello, Ada. Which line has the bug?
functions-11.explain: The function gives back a text, so its type must be `greet :: String -> String`.
functions-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-12.pairs.1: type of a function from `Int` to `Int`
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Compare values and choose a result with if, guards, pattern matching and case.
conditions.lesson.0: Comparisons give a `Bool`: `==` means equal, `/=` not equal, and there are `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. `&&` means and, `||` means or, and `not` turns `True` into `False` and `False` into `True`.
conditions.lesson.3: `if` chooses between two values. In Haskell, `if` always needs both `then` and `else`, because it must give back a value in every case.
conditions.lesson.5: A negative number as an argument needs parentheses. `describe -3` means `describe - 3`, a subtraction, and gives an error. Write `describe (-3)`.
conditions.lesson.7: With several cases, **guards** are clearer. Each guard starts with `|`, followed by a condition, `=` and the result. Haskell checks the guards from top to bottom and takes the first one that is `True`. `otherwise` is always `True` and catches all other cases.
conditions.lesson.10: You can also write a function as several equations for concrete values. Haskell uses the first equation whose **pattern** fits. The pattern `_` fits any value.
conditions.lesson.12: `case ... of` does the same inside an expression. Each line has a pattern, `->` and the result.
conditions.card.1: `if c then a else b` always needs `else`
conditions.card.2: `| x > 0 = ...` is a guard, `otherwise` catches the rest
conditions-1.explain: `/=` means not equal. 10 is not equal to 5, so the result is `True`.
conditions-2.explain: `0` is neither greater nor less than `0`, so only `otherwise` is left.
conditions-3.explain: The guards are checked from top to bottom. `12 > 10` is `True`, so the first guard wins and the others are not checked.
conditions-4.explain: `5` does not fit `0` or `1`. The pattern `_` fits any value.
conditions-5.statement: In Haskell, you can write an `if` without an `else` part to choose a value.
conditions-5.explain: `if` must give back a value in every case, so `else` is required.
conditions-6.explain: `/=` is `True` when the two values are different. Other languages often write `!=`.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the guard so that all other numbers give "other".
conditions-7.explain: `otherwise` is always `True`, so the last guard catches every remaining value.
conditions-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints yes.
conditions-8.explain: The parts are `if`, the condition, `then` with the first value and `else` with the second.
conditions-9.prompt: Build the result of parity so it gives `"even"` for even numbers and `"odd"` for all others.
conditions-9.explain: A number is even if the remainder of the division by 2 is `0`. `if` needs both `then` and `else`.
conditions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that size gives `"small"` below 10, `"medium"` below 100 and `"large"` for all other numbers.
conditions-10.explain: The guards are checked from top to bottom, so `n < 10` must come before `n < 100`. `otherwise` comes last.
conditions-11.prompt: The function should give "adult" for 18 and older. Which line has the bug?
conditions-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Store several values in a list, build lists with ranges, and use length, sum, take and more.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds several values of the same type, in square brackets and separated by commas. `[1, 2, 3]` has the type `[Int]`. A `String` is a list of characters: `"abc"` is the same as `['a', 'b', 'c']`.
lists.lesson.3: `[1 .. 5]` is the list of the numbers from 1 to 5. With a second value, you set the step: `[2, 4 .. 10]` counts in steps of 2. Ranges also work backwards and with characters.
lists.lesson.6: `:` puts one element in front of a list, and `++` joins two lists. Both give back a new list. The old list stays as it was.
lists.lesson.9: `reverse` turns a list around. `take n` gives the first `n` elements, and `drop n` gives the list without them. `elem x` checks whether `x` is in the list, and `null` checks whether the list is empty. `!!` gives the element at a position, starting at `0`.
lists.lesson.11: `!!` with a position that does not exist stops the program with an error, for example `[1, 2, 3] !! 5`.
lists.lesson.12: All elements of a list have the same type, so `[1, "two"]` is an error. In the next unit, you learn about tuples, which can hold values of different types.
lists.card.2: `0 : xs` adds in front, `xs ++ ys` joins
lists-1.explain: `length` counts the elements, not their values.
lists-2.explain: The first two values set the step to 2. The range stops at `9`.
lists-4.explain: `:` puts the element in front of the list.
lists-5.explain: Strings are lists of characters, so `++` joins them into one string without a space.
lists-6.explain: A `String` is a list of `Char` values. The double quotes are a short way to write it.
lists-7.explain: All elements of a list must have the same type. `1` is a number and `"two"` is a `String`.
lists-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 15.
lists-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints True.
lists-9.explain: `elem 3` checks whether `3` is in the list. `"3"` is a list of characters, not of numbers.
lists-10.prompt: Build an expression that gives the list [5,4,3,2,1].
lists-10.explain: `[1 .. 5]` gives the numbers from 1 to 5, and `reverse` turns the list around.
lists-11.prompt: The program should print the first three letters of the word. Which line has the bug?
lists-11.explain: `take` gets the number first and then the list: `print (take 3 word)`.
lists-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists-12.pairs.4: checks if the list is empty
recursion.title: Recursion and tuples
recursion.summary: Repeat work with recursive functions, take lists apart with patterns, and group values in tuples.
recursion.lesson.0: Haskell has no loops. To repeat something, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case** that ends it.
recursion.lesson.2: `factorial 3` becomes `3 * factorial 2`, then `3 * 2 * factorial 1`, then `3 * 2 * 1 * factorial 0`. The base case gives `1`, so the result is `6`.
recursion.lesson.4: A list is either empty, `[]`, or a first element in front of the rest, `x : xs`. A function on lists usually has one equation for each case. In the pattern `(x : xs)`, `x` is the first element and `xs` is the rest of the list.
recursion.lesson.8: A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values, which can have different types. `("Ada", 36)` has the type `(String, Int)`. `fst` gives the first part of a pair and `snd` the second. Patterns can take tuples apart, too.
recursion.lesson.10: `zip` combines two lists into one list of pairs.
recursion.lesson.12: If the base case is never reached, the recursion does not end. `factorial (-1)` counts down past `0` and never reaches the base case.
recursion.lesson.13: If a function has no equation for a value, the program stops with an error when it gets that value. Write an equation for every case, for example for `[]`.
recursion.card.0: `f 0 = 1` is the base case, `f n = n * f (n - 1)`
recursion.card.2: `(x : xs)` matches the first element and the rest
recursion-1.explain: Each element adds 1, and the empty list gives 0: 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
recursion-3.explain: `snd` gives the second part of the pair.
recursion-4.explain: Each step puts `n` in front of the rest. The base case `countdown 0` gives the empty list, so `0` is not in the result.
recursion-5.prompt: Which line is the base case?
recursion-5.explain: `total [] = 0` does not call `total` again. It ends the recursion.
recursion-6.statement: A tuple can hold values of different types, like `("Ada", 36)`.
recursion-6.explain: Unlike a list, a tuple can mix types. Its type lists them all: `(String, Int)`.
recursion-7.statement: In the pattern `(x : xs)`, `xs` is the last element of the list.
recursion-7.explain: `xs` is the rest of the list, everything after the first element `x`.
recursion-8.prompt: Complete the base case so that total [1, 2, 3] gives 6.
recursion-8.explain: The sum of an empty list is `0`. With `1`, every result would be one too big.
recursion-9.prompt: Complete the pattern so that firstOf gives the first element.
recursion-9.explain: The first element comes before `:`. A pattern with `:` needs parentheses.
recursion-10.prompt: Build the recursive equation of total.
recursion-10.explain: The sum is the first element plus the sum of the rest.
recursion-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Ada is here.
recursion-11.explain: `name` takes the first part of `person`, so `person` must be defined before it.
recursion-12.prompt: The function should count the elements of a list. Which line has the bug?
recursion-12.explain: An empty list has no elements: `count [] = 0`. With `1`, every result is one too big.
higher-order.title: Higher-order functions
higher-order.summary: Pass functions to functions: transform lists with map, filter and foldr, lambdas and list comprehensions.
higher-order.lesson.0: In Haskell, functions are values, so you can pass a function to another function. `map` applies a function to every element of a list and gives back the new list.
higher-order.lesson.2: `filter` keeps only the elements for which a function gives `True`. `even` and `odd` are such functions: they check whether a number is even or odd.
higher-order.lesson.5: A **lambda** is a function without a name. `\x -> x * x` takes `x` and gives back `x * x`. Lambdas are useful for short functions that you need only once.
higher-order.lesson.7: An operator with one side filled in is a function, too: `(+ 1)` adds 1, `(* 2)` doubles a number, and `(> 5)` checks whether a number is greater than 5.
higher-order.lesson.10: `foldr` combines all elements of a list into one value. `foldr (+) 0 [1, 2, 3]` computes `1 + (2 + (3 + 0))`. `(+)` is the operator `+` used as a function, and `0` is the start value.
higher-order.lesson.12: A **list comprehension** builds a list in one expression. `[x * x | x <- [1 .. 5], odd x]` reads: `x * x` for every `x` from 1 to 5 for which `odd x` is `True`.
higher-order.card.0: `map f xs` applies `f` to every element
higher-order.card.1: `filter even xs` keeps the matching elements
higher-order-2.explain: `filter` keeps the elements less than 4 and keeps their order.
higher-order-4.explain: The lambda adds 10 to every element. `map` keeps the length of the list.
higher-order-5.explain: Only `3` and `4` are greater than 2. Each of them is doubled.
higher-order-6.statement: `filter` can change the elements of a list, for example double them.
higher-order-6.explain: `filter` only keeps or removes elements. To change them, use `map`.
higher-order-7.explain: `map` applies `length` to each string: `"a"` has 1 character and `"bcd"` has 3.
higher-order-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints [2,4,6].
higher-order-8.explain: `map` applies `(* 2)` to every element. `filter` needs a function that gives a `Bool`.
higher-order-9.prompt: Complete the lambda so the program prints [1,4,9].
higher-order-9.explain: A lambda starts with a backslash, followed by its parameter and `->`.
higher-order-10.prompt: Build an expression that keeps the even numbers from 1 to 10.
higher-order-10.explain: `filter` gets the test `even` first and then the list.
higher-order-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints [20,40].
higher-order-11.explain: First the list, then the even numbers from it, then each of them times 10.
higher-order-12.prompt: The program should print the squares of the numbers. Which line has the bug?
higher-order-12.explain: `filter` only keeps or removes elements. To change each element, use `map`: `print (map (\x -> x * x) numbers)`.
types.title: Your own types
types.summary: Define your own data types with constructors and records, and handle missing values with Maybe.
types.lesson.0: With `data`, you define your own type. The type `Color` below has three possible values, its **constructors**. Types and constructors start with an uppercase letter. `deriving (Show, Eq)` lets you print the values and compare them with `==`. Without `Show`, `print` does not work for your type.
types.lesson.2: Functions on your type use pattern matching, with one equation for each constructor.
types.lesson.5: A constructor can carry values. `Circle Double` holds a radius, and `Rectangle Double Double` holds a width and a height. In a pattern, you give names to these values. `pi` is the number π.
types.lesson.8: With **record syntax**, every field has a name. The field names are also functions that read the field.
types.lesson.11: Sometimes there is no result. The type `Maybe` has two constructors: `Just x` holds a value, and `Nothing` holds none. A function that can fail gives back a `Maybe`, and `case` checks which one you got.
types.lesson.13: A `Maybe Int` is not an `Int`. To use the number, take it out first with pattern matching, for example with `case`.
types.card.2: `data Shape = Circle Double`, match it with `(Circle r)`
types-1.explain: `deriving Show` lets `print` show the constructor by its name.
types-2.explain: `Square 5` fits the first equation, so `s` is `5` and the result is 5 * 5.
types-3.explain: The field name `pages` is a function that reads the field.
types-4.explain: `"Bob"` does not fit the first equation, so the second one gives `Nothing`.
types-5.explain: `Later Int` holds a number, for example `Later 3`. `Yes` and `No` hold nothing.
types-6.statement: `Nothing` is a value of the type `Maybe Int`.
types-6.explain: A `Maybe Int` is either `Just` with a number or `Nothing`.
types-7.statement: Without `deriving Show`, you can print values of your own type with `print`.
types-7.explain: `print` needs `Show`. Without it, the compiler reports an error.
types-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Just 4.
types-8.explain: `Just` wraps a value into a `Maybe`. `Maybe` is the name of the type, not a constructor.
types-9.prompt: Complete the type so the program works.
types-9.explain: `|` separates the constructors of a type.
types-10.prompt: Build a type Weather with the values Hot and Cold.
types-10.explain: `data` starts the definition, and `|` separates the constructors.
types-11.prompt: The function should give the area of a shape. Which line has the bug?
types-11.explain: A constructor with its values needs parentheses in a pattern: `area (Square s) = s * s`.
types-12.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
